learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of applied thermodynamics and heat transfer. Basic principles and their application to solving engineering problems.
Basic knowledge and application of environmental technologies and sustainability.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.

Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning, and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Mechanical Industrial Engineering.
Ability to analyze and assess the social and environmental impact of technical solutions.
Ability to work in a multilingual and multidisciplinary environment.
Ability to analyze and synthesize.
Ability to organize and plan time.
Ability for written expression.
Ability to solve problems.
Ability for critical reasoning/logical analysis.

Students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is typically at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes aspects implying knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

Students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies typically demonstrated by elaborating and defending arguments and solving problems within their area of study.
Students have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their area of study) to make judgments that include reflection on relevant social, scientific, or ethical issues.
Students can transmit information, ideas, problems, and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Students have developed the learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.
Knowledge of the fundamental concepts, principles, and laws of Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer.
Knowledge and conceptual mastery related to the thermodynamic and thermophysical properties involved in the analysis of thermal systems and the analysis of heat transfer mechanisms.

Knowledge of the basic conservation laws and their application to mass and energy balances for the analysis of thermal equipment and systems, as well as the ability to formulate appropriate hypotheses and perform associated calculations.

Knowledge of the non-conservation laws derived from the application of the Second Principle of Thermodynamics and their theoretical and practical consequences, both in general terms and in specific terms for equipment and systems commonly used in Engineering.

Knowledge of the fundamentals of thermal systems based on thermodynamic cycles and the ability to perform calculations related to their analysis, as well as to assess the influence of their operation on the environmental impacts they generate.
Knowledge of the characteristics of each heat transfer mechanism, its application to practical cases of interest, and the ability to develop associated calculations.
Knowledge about the application of computer programs or online tools to solve problems related to the contents of Thermal Engineering.
Ability to structure the resolution of a problem systematically.
Ability to combine individual autonomy with collaborative group work.
Ability for adequate organization and work planning.
Ability for autonomous learning, being able to learn what is necessary to solve a problem.
Ability to prepare a formally rigorous written report.
Ability to formulate and apply simplifying hypotheses to problem-solving.
Ability for critical analysis of results, being able to detect calculation errors or modify working hypotheses.

syllabus_topics: General concepts of Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer
Properties
Relationships between properties
Simple idealized models for pure substances
Principles of Thermodynamics
Heat transfer mechanisms: general characteristics, parameters and fundamental laws
Thermal resistance
General formulation of an energy balance
Analysis and characterization of basic equipment: cylinder-piston, turbines, compressors, pumps, heat exchangers, nozzles, diffusers, combustion chambers, throttling valve
Energy balance in heat transfer
General formulation of an entropy balance
Entropy generation and exergy destruction (Gouy-Stodola theorem)
Analysis of basic equipment
Isentropic efficiencies
General formulation of an exergy balance
Ideal cycles and basic parameters related to steam thermal power plants
Ideal cycles and basic parameters related to gas turbine engines
Ideal cycles and basic parameters related to refrigeration systems
Ideal cycles and basic parameters related to heat pump systems
Basic aspects of environmental impacts in facilities associated with these cycles
Analysis of heat transfer through a composite plane wall
Analysis of heat transfer in a pipe with thermal insulation
Associated thermal circuits
Use of correlations for estimating convection coefficients in different cases of interest (different geometries, natural and forced convection, internal and external conduction)
Polytropic compression in a cylinder-piston
Compressor with cooling jacket
Analysis of a combustion engine
Thermodynamic analysis of the operation cycle of a steam thermal power plant
Thermodynamic analysis of a vapor compression refrigeration system
Turbojet engine for air propulsion
Heat loss through a composite wall
Thermodynamic analysis of a turbine with intermediate steam extraction
Analysis of steady-state heat transfer: plane wall and cylindrical pipe
Use of thermodynamic tables and diagrams
Study of ideal gas model limitations. Use of generalized compressibility chart
Heat transfer in an insulated chamber
Study of a simple vapor compression refrigeration system
Measurement of liquid heat capacity. Incompressible substance model
Measurement of convection coefficient by stationary heat generation
Generating tables and diagrams with the NIST WebBook tool
Cycle analysis with the Termograf tool
teaching_methods: Autonomous and collaborative group work on problems
Completion of online tasks and computer exercises
Exercises from recommended bibliography and virtual classroom
Use of the virtual classroom for course organization
Presentation of lab guides and work instructions
Individual and group note-taking during practical sessions
Use of bibliography and reading documents in English

assessment_methods.method: Exam of Task 1: Thermodynamic analysis of a turbine with intermediate steam extraction
Questionnaire of Task 2: Analysis of steady-state heat transfer: plane wall and cylindrical pipe
Preparation and lab work (including preparation activities and lab work for P1-P6)

assessment_rules: To pass the subject under continuous assessment, a grade of 5.0 or higher must be obtained in each of the two main blocks: EC1 (Problem Solving, 65%) and EC2 (Laboratory Practices, 35%). The final exam (EC1.3, 50% of the total grade) is divided into two parts: Part I (40%) requires a minimum grade of 4.0 for Part II (60%) to be corrected; if Part I is not passed, the maximum final exam grade is 0.4 * Part I grade. If Part II is not passed (minimum 4.0), the final exam grade is calculated as 0.4 * Part I + 0.6 * Part II, but capped at a maximum of 4.0. Students who do not pass in the first call will be evaluated under the single evaluation (EU) mode in a second call, which consists of two evaluation dates. The written practical test (EC2.2, 15%) requires a minimum grade of 5.0 and can be recovered once, either during the first or second call, but not simultaneously with the main EU exam. Grave conceptual errors or absurd results will invalidate the evaluation.
